summary: This standards-track document defines DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options that give a client its coordinate-based location: latitude, longitude, and altitude, with resolution indicators and the reference datum. A network can tell a device where it is as part of normal address setup.

eli5.summary: When your device joins a network, the network can also tell it where on the map it is, using the same message that gives it an address.

subtitle: How a DHCP server hands a client its latitude, longitude and altitude, with a stated margin of error.

tldr.problem: A device that joins a network often has no good way to learn where it physically is, yet applications such as emergency telephony need a caller's location to pick the right emergency center.
tldr.mechanism: DHCPv4 and DHCPv6 options carry latitude, longitude and altitude as fixed-point numbers, each with a resolution or uncertainty value, plus a datum field that says which coordinate reference system the numbers use.
tldr.outcome: A DHCP client gets its coordinate-based location during normal address configuration and keeps it on the device. This RFC obsoletes RFC 3825 and adds the uncertainty-based GeoLoc options.

today: RFC 6225 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2011. It obsoletes RFC 3825, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why Hand Out Location Through DHCP
sections.content:
The physical location of a network device has many uses. The RFC singles out emergency telephony, which relies on knowing where a caller is in order to choose the correct emergency center.

Location can be given as geodetic coordinates or as a civic address, and both forms may be used at once. This document covers the coordinate form for DHCPv4 and DHCPv6. Civic addresses are handled by RFC 4776.

For a wired Ethernet host, the server could work out the location from a wiremap, using the Circuit ID in the relay agent option from RFC 3046 to find where the circuit ends, such as a wall jack. The same mechanism can tell a wireless host where its access point is, or what area the access point covers. An important property is that once the DHCP exchange is done, the location is stored on the end device rather than somewhere that is hard to query.
sections.eli5: Imagine a hotel desk clerk who hands you a room key and also tells you which floor you are on. The network does the same: it gives your device an address and tells it where it is.

sections.title: Resolution and Uncertainty
sections.content:
Every location comes with a statement of how precise it is, in one of two styles. Resolution counts how many bits of each coordinate are valid. Uncertainty says how large the error is, as a distance from the encoded point to the furthest edge of the region where the target might be.

Uncertainty is given for each of the three axes separately, so the region it describes is a rectangular prism. When converting a more complex shape, the goal is the smallest prism this format can describe, so that the target is always inside it. The RFC notes that no inference about privacy policy can be drawn from either value.

For resolution, bits beyond the claimed resolution MAY be randomized to hide greater precision the sender might have. The RFC also describes conversions between these options and the PIDF-LO location format (RFC 4119, RFC 5491). Converting to PIDF-LO does not increase uncertainty. Converting from PIDF-LO to the GeoLoc options increases it by less than a factor of 2 in each dimension, and no conversion to the resolution-based option 123 is specified.
sections.eli5: If you say you live 'near the park', that is less exact than naming your street. These fields let the network say how exact its answer is, like saying 'I am sure to within a few steps'.

sections.title: The Three Option Formats
sections.content:
Three options are defined, all with the same basic layout and differing mainly in the option code:

  • DHCPv6 GeoLoc Option, option code 63.
  • DHCPv4 GeoLoc Option, code 144.
  • DHCPv4 GeoConf Option, code 123, originally defined in RFC 3825.

For version 1, the option length of the GeoLoc options is 16. Each option carries Latitude and Longitude as 34-bit fixed-point values, a 4-bit Altitude Type (AType), a 30-bit Altitude and a 3-bit Datum.

The GeoLoc options add a 2-bit Ver field, always at the same offset whatever the version, a 3-bit reserved Res field, and a 6-bit uncertainty field for each axis (LatUnc, LongUnc, AltUnc). The older GeoConf option instead has 6-bit resolution fields (LaRes, LoRes, AltRes) and a 5-bit Res field. The RFC says the former single Datum field was split into Ver, Res and Datum.
sections.eli5: The message is a small form with boxes for 'how far north', 'how far east', 'how high', and 'how sure are we'. Each box has a fixed size so every device reads it the same way.

sections.title: Encoding Coordinates and Altitude
sections.content:
Latitude and longitude are 34-bit two's complement fixed-point values with 9 integer bits and 25 fractional bits, rounded to the nearest representable value. Positive latitudes are north of the equator and positive longitudes are east of the Prime Meridian. For datums 1 to 3, longitudes outside -180 to 180 degrees or latitudes outside -90 to 90 degrees are invalid; location consumers MUST ignore them and SHOULD log an error.

Resolution (option 123): the value says how many high-order bits MUST be treated as valid. A value of 2 means a precision of no better than 1/6th of the globe, and 34 means about 3.11 mm in latitude at the equator (about 2.42 mm in longitude).

Uncertainty (options 63 and 144): the distance is 2 ^ (8 - x) degrees for an encoded value x. A value of 0 means unknown, and values above 34 are reserved. The encoder picks x = 8 - ceil(log2(uncertainty)), which rounds the uncertainty up to the next power of two. Uncertainty applies to each axis independently.

Altitude depends on AType: 0 means no known altitude (the field MUST be ignored), 1 means meters and 2 means floors. Both use a 30-bit two's complement value with 22 integer bits and 8 fractional bits. Floors are relative to ground level, negative below it, and a mezzanine between floor 1 and floor 2 could be written as 1.25. Altitude uncertainty is 2 ^ (21 - x) and applies only to type 1.
sections.eli5: Numbers are stored like a ruler with tiny marks. The 'how sure' number says how many marks you can trust, and floors can even be fractions, so a half-floor landing is 4.5.

sections.title: Datums and Who Must Support What
sections.content:
The Datum field says how coordinates relate to the real world. Three are defined:

  • 1: WGS84 (latitude, longitude, altitude), identified by EPSG code 4979, or 4326 without altitude.
  • 2: NAD83 horizontal plus the NAVD88 vertical datum, for land (not near tidal water) in North America.
  • 3: NAD83 horizontal plus the MLLW (Mean Lower Low Water) vertical datum, for locations on or near tidal water in North America.

All hosts MUST support WGS84. A DHCP client that does not understand a datum value MUST assume WGS84 and proceed, on the reasoning that a less accurate location is better than none.

DHCPv4 clients MUST support receiving GeoLoc Option 144 (version 1) and MAY support GeoConf Option 123. DHCPv6 clients MUST support receiving version 1 responses, and DHCPv6 servers MUST send version 1.

On the server side, a DHCPv4 server MUST support sending option 144 version 1 and SHOULD support sending option 123. It SHOULD honor the client's Parameter Request List when deciding whether to send option 123, option 144 or both.
sections.eli5:
A map can be drawn in different ways, like measuring height from the floor or from sea level. The datum tells you which way the numbers were measured.

New devices must know how to read the newer form. The older form is optional, like still being able to read an old map style.

sections.title: Security and Privacy
sections.content:
DHCP messages have no privacy protection, so an eavesdropper on the link between the server and the client can read the location. To limit exposure, the server SHOULD return the option only when the client has asked for it in its Parameter Request List.

Where critical decisions depend on the value, DHCP authentication (RFC 3118 for DHCPv4 and the mechanism in RFC 3315 for DHCPv6) SHOULD be used to protect integrity. Link-layer confidentiality and integrity protection may also help. The RFC points to the Geopriv requirements (RFC 3693) for the wider security discussion.
sections.eli5: Anyone listening in on the network wire could overhear where you are. So the server only tells you if you ask, and locks the message if it really matters.

sections.title: IANA Registries
sections.content:
IANA assigned DHCPv6 option code 63 (OPTION_GEOLOCATION) and DHCPv4 code 144 (GeoLoc, data length 16), and created three registries, all with new assignments by Standards Action.

The Altitude Type registry holds values 0 to 2, with 3 to 15 unassigned. The Datum registry reserves 0, assigns 1 to 3 and leaves 4 to 7 unassigned. The GeoLoc Option Version registry reserves 0, assigns 1 and leaves 2 and 3 unassigned.
sections.eli5: IANA keeps the official lists of which number means what, so everyone's devices agree.

sections.title: Changes From RFC 3825
sections.content:
This RFC obsoletes RFC 3825. It defines a DHCPv6 GeoLoc option and a new DHCPv4 GeoLoc option, splits the old Datum field into Ver, Res and Datum, adds client and server support requirements, and adds sections on latitude, longitude and altitude fields, resolution, uncertainty and datums.

Appendix A maps the options to GML shapes (a point, a polygon or a prism, depending on which fields are present), and appendices B and C work through resolution and uncertainty examples.
sections.eli5: This is the updated edition. It adds a new, easier way to say how sure the location is and tidies up the old rules.

fields.desc: Option version; this RFC defines version 1.

fields.desc: Map datum used for the coordinates.

items.label: WGS84
items.desc: Latitude, longitude, altitude; EPSG 4979, or 4326 without altitude.

items.label: NAD83 + NAVD88
items.desc: Land, not near tidal water, in North America.

items.label: NAD83 + MLLW
items.desc: On or near tidal water in North America.
